analysis.title: Precious Analyst: Long-Term Constructive Gold, But Just Not Today
key_insights: GS lowers its end-2026 gold forecast to $4,150/toz (from $4,650) and its end-2027 forecast to $4,800/toz (from $5,400), citing the Fed's hawkish shift in recent months and its effect on investor positioning.

Structural central bank demand stays the core of the long-term bull case. GS assumes 60 tonnes/month through 2026-27, against a 3-month seasonally adjusted nowcast of 85 tonnes/month now and a pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes/month. This drives most of the 15% price upside GS forecasts by end-2027.

GS's base case includes a December 2026 Fed hike. It expects this to keep investor 'debasement concerns' contained, so macro-policy hedge demand (seen in call-option demand) normalizes toward its historical average instead of returning to the elevated levels of early 2026.
GS says the current setup increasingly resembles 2022: central banks provide a strong structural bid, but higher rates weigh on investor positioning, so gold rises at a more modest pace on net.

GS expects three Fed cuts from late 2027 through early 2028. That should remove the rate constraint on gold and let Western gold ETF inflows compete with central bank buying again, turning that buying more fully into higher prices.

Downside risk to the forecast comes from a potential additional March 2027 hike, delayed cuts and/or a higher terminal rate. With an extra March hike and a higher terminal rate, GS estimates gold at $4,660/toz by end-2027.

Upside beyond the $4,800 base case could come from revived macro-policy hedge demand if DM fiscal sustainability concerns grow, including higher military spending and rising debt in energy-importing countries, and investors doubt how DM central banks would respond.

For CTAs and macro hedge funds, the next 3-6 months remain challenging. Reasons given are a rising funds rate, volatile energy prices, volatility around inflation and labor-market data, and tight drawdown limits. Higher oil could add systematic selling, and sharp equity drawdowns could first pull gold lower through margin calls and deleveraging.
For longer-horizon investors seeking central bank demand exposure or protection against macro policy tail risks, GS says the current correction in gold may offer a more attractive entry point.

EM central banks, particularly China, remain underweight gold relative to plausible long-term allocations. DM central banks have largely sat out the buying wave since 2022, but the debate is shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, which points to reserve security concerns.

GS's gold model assumes each 100 tonnes of net conviction demand (Western ETF holdings, net managed money positioning and central bank purchases) raises gold about 2%. Since mid-2025 price moves have been larger than flows alone imply, coinciding with a sharp rise in call-option demand.

GS estimates a 1 million contract increase in net GLD call open interest adds roughly 5% to gold prices. The beta on conviction demand rises with call-option positioning relative to historical norms, likely reflecting dealer-hedging amplification.

Call-option amplification is not included in the base-case forecast because the history of elevated call demand is short and the effect size is uncertain. It could return in the upside case once the hiking cycle ends and the rate constraint fades.

charts_described: Exhibit 3: GS nowcast of central bank gold purchases at 85 tonnes/month on a 3-month seasonally adjusted basis, versus a pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes.
Exhibit 6: an additional March hike and higher terminal rate imply $4,660/toz by end-2027, while renewed macro-policy hedging as rates fall in 2027H2 provides upside to the $4,800 base case.
vol_and_positioning: GS proxies call-option demand with net GLD call open interest relative to puts. It notes this captures only part of the market because of substantial OTC activity.
Call-option demand rose sharply from mid-2025 and is read as a macro-policy or 'debasement' hedge, meaning investors paying for exposure to a non-linear gold rally.
Dealers who have sold calls may need to buy gold as it approaches key strikes, reinforcing rallies. When gold falls they may unwind hedges, amplifying the downside.
GS expects call-option demand to normalize toward historical levels during the hiking cycle, not return to the extremes of early 2026.
CTAs and macro funds face tight drawdown limits, which make long gold positions hard to hold over the next 3-6 months.
geopolitical: Higher military spending and rising debt burdens in energy-importing countries could add to DM fiscal sustainability concerns.
Motivations for diversifying away from G7 reserve currencies, including geopolitical and financial risk, likely remain in place.
Debate among central banks is shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, pointing to concerns over reserve security and cross-country trust.

tension_points.bull_case: Structural central bank buying (85 tonnes/month nowcast, 60 assumed vs 17 pre-2022), possible revival of macro-policy hedge demand if DM fiscal worries grow, and three Fed cuts from late 2027 lifting gold toward and above $4,800.
tension_points.bear_case: A hawkish Fed with a December 2026 hike weighs on investor positioning and keeps call-option demand normalizing lower. An additional March 2027 hike or higher terminal rate would put gold near $4,660 by end-2027.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An additional March 2027 hike, delayed cuts and/or a higher terminal rate would push GS's end-2027 forecast down to $4,660/toz.
